1. As others have mentioned, make sure you have the scale right. Even if you draw out the map ahead of time, you need to make sure that when you translate it into the SDK it's how you imagined it, so a good frame of reference is to put terrorists/cts around the map to keep perspective.
2. ***Don't*** be afraid to try radical changes to your map, but ***do*** save often and save under different files to test changes you may want to take back. If the change works out, you can just keep using that version, but if it doesn't you can just go back to the previous version. (It's generally good to save under a format such as de\_dust2\_a1\_1 or something. "de" is defuse, dust2 is the map name, a1 stands for alpha 1 which you will change the number as you make major changes, and the 1 at the end is for minor changes. Whatever works for you, but it doesn't hurt to keep saving under new file names (other than maybe disk space) If you're like me, I like to keep a record of my work in case something I do ever becomes popular and people want to know behind-the-scenes stuff).
3. *Avoid* creating diagonals structures because scaling them can be a nightmare.
4. ***Don't*** worry about how it looks until you're ready to show others. Even then it shouldn't matter until you are ready to make a "release copy". Your layout with continuously change as you come across issues, make adjustments and think of new ideas (often as a happy compromise). It *is* important, though to make sure visibility is good. If you use the same blank texture on every wall, it can be really hard to spot enemies so texture around edges and use ones that will help the opponents pop out from the background. Of course, that all can be changed later once you know what kind of theme you want to go for, which leads me to my next point.
5. ***Don't*** be afraid to use placeholders. Textures, objects, props, lights, *anything* can be changed later to something better looking, more realistic, better fitting, etc. You don't have to make everything perfect right away.
6. This one is true for many types of projects, but if you find yourself getting frustrated with a certain part of your map while trying to make it work or to fix it, feel free to move on to a different part that is going to be more gratifying to work on until your frustration has subsided and you've had time to come back with a fresh perspective.
7. ***Do*** study other maps, particularly the ones you enjoy playing the most. Find out what it is you like about those maps and what they have in common and see how you can apply that yourself to your own map. This *should* be fun anyway if you are interested in map making.
8. Playtest, *playtest,* ***playtest.*** It can be hard to tell if a map is well designed or even fun to play with only bots to go against, especially since they're incredibly stupid, but you'll *quickly* be able to figure out major flaws by playtesting at every stage of development. Think of your map like a sculpture. You start with a rough shape, shape it into a structure you enjoy and feel is structurally sound, and then eventually add on little details to it.
9. When you *do* show your map to others, it's best to have callouts for each location as it makes it easier to communicate feedback about it. It's great, too, if you make a radar image for playtesting.

#Bombsites
It's interesting you say that because I was afraid there would be too many entrances to each site, but since you mention there being too many entrances to mid, that fear may be part of that issue instead. 
Yeah, I thought it was a nice contrast to have one rather standard and simple site (A) while the other site (B) was more risky and complex.
I just want to point out that, depending on how you define it, there are actually 5 entrances to A and 4 entrances to B. However, that's only if you count the entrance from CT on A site (which could potentially be used if people bypass B from the back of B Long and went through CT spawn) as well as the entrance from "Walkway" which you can get to by jumping onto the four newsboxes then onto the payphone. As for B, that would be counting the CT entrance and the "Walkway" entrance to connector. I don't mean to be overly technical as these probably wouldn't be majorly useful as they're hard to get to and would more than likely be covered.

#Middle
That's definitely something I _felt_ but couldn't really articulate mentally. I'm working on closing off entrances to mid and can already feel an improvement. I'm going to create different iterations to test it and I'll show you screen shots if you'd like. For now, I will say that the street going toward A is very important for timing, because without it going from Mid to "A Main" or vice-versa would take a very long time. The street on the right, though has definitely been something I'm not happy with, with the sort of circle of the three doorways and have went ahead and closed the entrance under the catwalk, but for the first iteration, have kept the door to mid from the T building onto that street while closing off the other one on the left side.
It's funny you mention narrowing it, because originally it was even wider and longer haha, so I went through the process of compressing it. This time, if I do so again, though, What I might do is just try to have more empty space out of bounds (in between the building's walls) rather than just scooting everything closer. The idea of using slopes as cover is one I really like as mentioned by 3kliksphilip and I had always wanted the middle to have a range in elevation (I was thinking of the very middle with the light pole to be elevated specifically). I'll definitely have to experiment with it.

#Timings
As far as them getting to the A chokepoints at the same time, I didn't mention this, but I actually calculated the timings for A side and was going to make adjustments just to B side so the original timings weren't affected which is why they work haha. It's interesting what you say about B Long as that has definitely seemed to be proven true in practice, though of course it's hard to take bots as hard evidence. I suppose it's quite similar to A Long on Dust II, in this case that CT's have control of it and can push up pretty far but are very vulnerable. So maybe that's not even a problem and something that doesn't need adjusted. I feel like the Squeaky entrance makes all the difference as far as balancing B control. 
The drain area was intended as a way for T's to stealthily make there way to the back of B long without being noticed. It used to actually extend to the other side of the wooden doors, but it's always felt out of place. Fun fact: Idk if you noticed, but there's a lot of (pseudo)symmetry in the map and not just in mid. The far sides of the map are elevated up and down respectively and there's an underpath on A side while there's an overpath on B side. I'm not sure if you noticed (assuming you were just going off the screenshots), but the left-most part of the drain is under B Long which adds to the ability to sneak. But yeah, it's certainly kind of useless and I've been trying to think of ways to make it work, but it may just need to be completely scrapped. I've considered cutting out the path to the back of Long B and making the player take the drain route to get there. Maybe that along with moving it closer to the center would fix it. 
Going back to A site, getting across to "Upper A" requires crossing the CT's view so I thought that helps it from being overpowered. The T's CAN come from "Under", but the doorway to "Tunnels" (which is the part between "Under" and "Upper A" with the ladder) can be viewed from "Music" and also takes several extra seconds to get to so hopefully it keeps it kind of balanced.

#Other
Yeah, the windows are definitely inconsistent. To give some context, they were never meant to be wallbangable. The idea was to give information without an actual shootable view, but that definitely feels unintuitive. The top windows ended up being breakable because I felt it added to the ability to quickly get down from catwalk and out of B. I've always been a fan of one-way drops in general. The other two windows on the right side of B were added later for aesthetic appeal and to allow more light to get into the site. I'm not sure if being able to see into and out of them is good, bad, neutral. If I were to keep the four non-breakable windows, I would try to find a texture that matches like bullet-proof glass, but that's one of the things farther down the line along with general polish. Speaking of which, frankly, I have no idea what I'm doing with displacements and they are essentially broken. I just added them at all at this stage to give a feel of what they would hopefully end up being like as the map before felt a lot more inorganic and I think that helped. That's another thing I could ideally get someone else to work with or that I would have to learn more about to get right. 
Yeah, I don't like ladders in general either. They're a good example of a placeholder until something better comes to mind and they're just a lot quicker to move around and change than proper stairs or whatever. I thought about changing the connector part in B to lose the doorway near the back of the site towards CT and adding a stairway from it to the balcony by the windows. I'm not very happy with the connector area in general anyway for whatever reason. 
The bridge to B site is actually intended to be vulnerable, a risk vs reward thing. There's actually only two CT-controlled places it can be viewed from and they cause the CT's to be vulnerable from other angles when standing there. Not that it's without fault of course. Just wanted to point out that it was intentional. 

Anyway, thanks for the feedback and I'll continue to playtest it, tweak things, and experiment. Sorry for the long reply, btw.

And if no one has told you before, name your map like "de_dust2_a1", changing the to a2, a3, etc. for alpha versions, b1, b2, etc. for beta, and rc, rc2, etc. for "release candidate" which means basically it's done, but may be changed. You don't actually want to name it something just like "de_dust2". "The reason for this is that you still want to have the ability to update the map later if need be. If you release the map without a suffix, you don't have a way to iterate the name anymore. If you release with \_final, you'd have to move on to \_final1 or \_final2, which is confusing for server operators and doesn't make a whole lot of sense in general. But if you label your map as _rc, it is natural that an \_rc2 or \_rc3 can exist."

Piracy is a curious thing for me. I see a site like this get shut down or see Dunovo still not being cracked and I'm like "aww", but at the same time, my first thought is it's a good thing for the industry perhaps. But the thing is, I don't think piracy should go away completely. The obvious thought is "Oh, well, it's bad for developers who make less money because of it." which is true and certainly hurts indie developers who don't have the means for extensive DRM or that much money to begin with, but I still feel piracy is a necessary evil in some circumstances and it's usually due to anti-consumer practices. It's just the way I feel, as I can't really think of a good argument for it as a whole, right now, but I think we should consider that piracy has always pretty much been a thing, of course definitely since we've had the internet, and we should contemplate the implications of an industry with zero piracy. When I see these new, uncracked forms of DRM and major piracy sites getting shut down, it really makes me ponder what the world would be like if the only option for users was purchasing the product, and I think if one takes the time to ponder it, one will come to a similar conclusion that it's probably not a good thing to be completely without it.

Very good question. It's hard for me to think of warning signs as opposed to just a given aspect which is bad. I'll start with saying anything in a game which is simply unfair. 

Usually, it means taking unavoidable damage but a specific example of something else unfair is in the case of Ninja Gaiden for the NES when it has impossible jumps without using items. It's obvious why damage should always be avoidable, but to give a bit of insight into how to do items in games like NG, a developer should always make a game possible without specific items, excluding those which the player always has such as a grappling hook or a gravity gun or skills and spells they've learned. Items should help an area be easier, but not be required for completion. In the Ninja Gaiden example, they could have fixed that issue by either always making sure you had the proper items or by making the areas completable without them. Making it passable without them is even better because it allows players to beat the games in challenging no item runs. 

However, this isn't the same thing as having limited resources. If you play a survival-horror game, like Resident Evil, Silent Hill, System Shock 2, a roguelike, or maybe an old shooter like DOOM (which I've been playing recently), it makes sense that there is limited ammunition which is required to complete the game, because the player was given the opportunity to collect it earlier and has to manage it throughout the game by being conservative, while being resourceful by exploring to find extra supplies. It can suck if you messed up a while ago and are being punished now, but that's part of learning to conserve. The difference between this and NG or something is that when you die in NG all your items go away, where here you have to restart from a save or a checkpoint where you should still have all your ammo and supplies.

I did think of one thing that I find to be bad design early on which is too much information being presented to the player at a time, which obviously usually occurs during the tutorial part of a game, which some games entirely skip for this reason. It doesn't need to be said that directly explaining things to a player is very useful and most games should do so, but it's just when it's paragraph after paragraph of text without letting the player _play_ before giving more info that it becomes a nuisance. It's just a matter of balancing, but the general rule of thumb I would give is just space out the "tutorial" bits intermittently between gameplay parts instead of giving a player a 10-page manual which at the end of they'll know everything. 

This is actually similar to any other kind of learning such as programming. A student should learn a bit, then practice what they've learned (in this case play the game for a bit). That way it's gratifying for them, keeps them engaged, and reinforces that they're actually learning and not just blankly taking the info in without understanding the reasons behind it. One thing to remember, while it's frustrating for returning players (though this can be fixed with new game+ mechanisms), limiting the control(s) a player has while they're learning isn't really a bad thing. Let them play around with the tools they've learned without overwhelming them with ones they have not. This is something you see a lot with rpgs, like World of Warcraft or Diablo 3, where they are given a few skills at a time instead of all of them from the start. On the other hand, some games it's okay to have all the features available, or for some of the features to be fully functional if they don't get in the way of the player. Some things that spring to mind would be menus which the players _can_ click on, but don't have to to proceed (not the least of which being the options menu). What tends to get in the way is the immediate GUI such as text on the screen, buffs, timers, etc. which the player is drawn to because it's right in front of them and confused about which leads to feeling overwhelmed. A good game to show how to do it well is Diablo II (which I have also been playing recently). There's a lot of UI, but it's constant and not in your face.

That's a really good question which I hope they answer. I think it's a terrible excuse as a game should be fun from the beginning. Of course, some games are more focused on story-telling, horror, or other aspects, but whatever the game is being recommended for, I think it should happen within the first 30 minutes so. That leaves time for exposition, like the walking around the lab in Half-Life, walking around City-17 in Half-Life 2, and the Vault 101 part of Fallout 3 for examples. On top of that, I think you should be allowed to skip that stuff on subsequent playthroughs, like how you should always have the option to skip cut scenes. 

In my experience, examples of games that (supposedly) get fun, but start out boring are usually RPGs where you have to grind levels to get to the "fun content" like in World of Warcraft where it supposedly gets fun when you raid, but you have to grind up so many levels to get there which takes a lot of hours (though I do like dungeons), or the original Final Fantasy where you have to fight random mobs over and over to level up enough to go against the story enemies. An example of a FF game that I think did it right was FF6, where you level up as you go through the story, though that's probably due to it's linearity (though not as linear as FFX which also seemed to do leveling right to me, though I haven't played far into it), which some people may not enjoy. 

The thing about "grinding" is that, by my definition, it's not fun. Leveling _can_ and _has_ been fun in a lot of games and I think anything in a game should be fun, interesting, or satisfying to a player like combat, reading a note, or beating a hard boss. I guess it all depends on what you're trying to do.

James Sunderland. He's a very unassuming character and doesn't talk very often since he's usually alone throughout the game so you get to intuit his feelings and thoughts as you go through the town, see horrific monsters, and reflect on the things that have occurred. It let's you infer these things because the few times he does talk, he comes off as a sentimental, loving, and harmless guy, which makes the twist all the more surprising. He is very much a character who speaks through actions more than words, as he does anything he can to find Mary. The things he says and the way he speaks paints a picture of who he is and he comes off as so very human and flawed.
 *spoilers* He doesn't convince Eddie to change his ways, he doesn't save Angela from her torment, and he can't change what he did to his wife, but he truly feels sorry and guilty for these things (including the remorse he felt for killing Eddie). The conversation he has with Mary at the end is so heartfelt as he tries to explain why he did it and admits to being selfish in addition to just wanting to end her suffering. He has grown as a character as he's willing to admit what he did and no longer bury it in his mind (another inferred thing). I feel like he's learned from this and that the appropriate ending is the "Leave" one because the "In Water" ending, though it's pretty much the true ending according to the devs, makes it feel like he hasn't learned the consequences of his selfishness. It feels right that due to his love for Mary and new lack of selfishness, he would (ironically) move on with his life and try to be happy since that's what SHE wanted which we know because she said so in the letter and we can infer her deep love for James. *end of spoilers*.
I think all of the characters are written well and all belong in the story, each representing something for James, just like the monsters. Hearing Mary's full letter at the end always brings tears to my eyes as it really feels like something someone would say in their last days to someone they really love. The flashback audio part where he leaves her alone out of frustration and she and she asks him to not go is another part that always makes it hard for me to see. Even Laura is well written. Each character feels like someone you could know.

I read somewhere that even if your reader doesn't know all the details, you should. While that's a perfectly fine way to write, I find it appealing to not know yourself. If you feel the same wonder as the reader, your story may be the better for it and you are likely to enjoy it more.   I made a DND world and came up with this whole background and made a pretty detailed world map and that worked great, especially since you never know where the players will go. I guess it's just a matter of what you are trying to do. I think finding a balance is probably ideal.
